newsitem.title: NEPAL: Germany to help Nepal stop child labour in carpets.
newsitem.headline: Germany to help Nepal stop child labour in carpets.

text.p: Germany, the largest buyer of Nepali carpets, will help the Himalayan kingdom stop the use of children in rug-making, a German official said on Tuesday.
"We would like to support the carpet industries to make them child labour free," Karl Kirchhof, leader of a German delegation, told Reuters.

Kirchhof, in Nepal for an annual meeting to review German aid, said Bonn was providing financial aid for marketing of carpets using the Rugmark label, which certifies carpets that are environmentally friendly and free of child labour.

Nepali officials said they had started initial work with the India-based Rugmark Foundation, which gives the label. "We have to go into the criteria acceptable to buyers," said Industry Ministry spokesman Bimal Koirala.

There are no statistics available on the extent of child labour in Nepal, one of the world's 10 poorest countries, but children are widely employed in making carpets. Woollen carpets are the country's leading export item.
Germany bought eight billion rupees ($141 million) worth of hand-knotted woollen carpets -- more than 80 percent of the kingdom's total export of rugs -- in fiscal 1993/94 (July 15-July 14).

But the exports dropped to 6.2 billion rupees ($110 million) in 1994/95 after German buyers cut back imports under pressure from consumer groups opposed to child labour and poor quality colouring chemicals.
Nepal has since prohibited the use of the inferior azo dye, which met with restrictions in Germany.
A Commerce Ministry official said carpet exports to Germany rose marginally to 6.4 billion rupees ($113.6 million) in 1995/96.
Germany is among the top aid donors to Nepal, which receives 60 percent of its development assistance in foreign grants.

German officials said the level of annual assistance, which is in the form of non-refundable grants, will be raised to $28 million (42 million marks) in 1996, up 40 percent from $20 million (30 million marks) last year.
